items.title: Websites in History: StumbleUpon
items.body:
Editor's note

Websites in History takes a nostalgic look at the sites that shaped how people use the internet today. Each edition hands the mic to a Squarespace contributor, who revisits one site from the archives and unpacks what it got right, what it got wrong, and what it still teaches us about building for the web. This edition comes from Tyler, Director of Global Content at Squarespace.

 

I don’t remember exactly when I stopped using StumbleUpon. It was likely sometime around 2007 or 2008, when Digg and Reddit came on the scene and internet discovery came pre-loaded with visible peer reviews and voting, making StumbleUpon feel too unpredictable for my declining digital risk tolerance.

At that moment in time, freshly out of my parents’ basement and living with roommates in the Central District of Seattle, I didn’t realize how much I would miss Stumbling.

StumbleUpon began in 2001, founded by a small group of programmers who had a simple, yet untapped, idea: instead of searching for a topic the way you would on Google, what if a website could help you discover new, weird, and wonderful websites? By sharing your interests and clicking a button, StumbleUpon would take you from page to page across the vast nodes of the internet, uncovering the world’s creativity one stumble at a time.

Stumbling, as it was called, caught on fast. StumbleUpon reached 2.3 million users by 2007. That number looks small today, but it’s worth mentioning virtually no one had a computer in their pocket. Napster, a service seemingly everyone used, only reached about 26.4 million users at its peak, a figure that would be a rounding error for Facebook today. But in 2007, 2.3 million was a big number.

As StumbleUpon evolved, it became a toolbar, then a browser extension, and then an app. It launched StumbleVideo and pseudo-white label versions that made it possible for users to stumble across MySpace and Flickr accounts, too. In other words, it diversified and innovated in the hunt for revenue. But its core value stayed intact. I could click the Stumble button and land on a website that could change my entire afternoon.

Ask any StumbleUpon devotee about their Stumbling and they’ll immediately invoke a website they found in detail, as if it were yesterday. I vividly remember Stumbling onto a site that had a map overlaid with haunted locations across the United States. I pulled up my hometown and neighboring towns, reading the likely invented lore and letting my imagination run wild. One entry was for a school where my mom worked, noting that a young boy had been seen walking the hallways late at night . . . which is what I did when my mom worked late grading tests . . . (Am I the ghost?) I kept that site open for days, poring over ghost stories from every state I’d lived in, along with the cities and hometowns of extended family, so I’d have material for our next family reunion. Then I clicked Stumble again and forgot the name of that site forever, because Homestar Runner popped up on the screen.

At Squarespace, we love websites, design, and building something worth discovering. We talk about websites, look at websites, and even make ads featuring Adam Driver saying the word websites over and over.

Explore Squarespace

As students of the website, we also recognize that the web, as it exists today, inherits the traits of the sites that came before it. By looking back at the websites of yore, we gain a better understanding of how the internet of today came to be. And while StumbleUpon wasn’t necessarily an exhibition of design virtuosity, its inner workings had significant implications for the current state of the web and how we exist within it.

Which brings me to surprise and delight.

I love talking about surprise and delight because a) I like being surprised and surprising (mostly) and b) being delighted and delighting (always). And surprise and delight, defined as something unexpected that gives a high degree of joy or satisfaction, is as much a part of successful website design as finding the right brand logo. Looking at StumbleUpon, the takeaway isn’t necessarily to develop a better algorithm for pairing user-generated content with customer data in an addictive format (although that’s StumbleUpon’s legacy), it’s about building a site that provides a genuinely human interaction, which, in a sea of impersonal sites, is delightful.

Many years ago, I audited a client’s website that looked like every other corporate site. Their weekly active users had dropped noticeably, and they were trying to understand why folks were interacting less with their site.

I dug in and noticed they’d removed a widget from their site a few days before engagement dropped off. The widget looped videos of extreme sports clips in the upper-left corner of the site. When I asked the company about it, they told me it felt unprofessional and antithetical to their (now) buttoned up brand. But when we interviewed their customers, it was clear people loved that video feed. It was entertaining, gave the brand a bit of an edge, and brought users back to the site because it reminded them the brand was more than a faceless entity.

For this brand’s audience, the video widget was a welcome surprise.

This isn’t to say everyone should add extreme sports clips to their site, but that little moment of surprise and delight endeared this brand to their users. When the widget returned, the usage rate returned with it.

What StumbleUpon delivered, and what its descendants still deliver today, is the promise of surprise and delight. I don’t scroll Reddit because I like content aggregators; I’m hunting for the feeling only a video of a kid relaying their love of turtles, corn, or some other equally cute thing can deliver.

Of course, StumbleUpon also helped give rise to the algorithmic content feed that shapes so much of how we browse today. StumbleUpon was addictive in a manner that’s familiar to any social media user, but it was slow and platformless, which meant content didn’t have to conform to any sort of algorithmic format or trend.

That’s not to say I didn’t spend an hour Stumbling from site to site. I absolutely did. But I had to actively engage with each one, evaluate its merits in juxtaposition of my interests and capacity for novelty (mileage varied), and then either spend the next 15 minutes smashing digital ants with a paperweight or learning about the physics of water or simply Stumbling on.

It was incredibly effective. Anyone who managed Google Analytics for a website in the early 2010s can attest that StumbleUpon surpassed Facebook in social media referral traffic. People pressed the stumble button over a billion times a month. People were Stumbling.

The state of the internet at the time had as much influence over my enjoyment of StumbleUpon as the site itself. When I say I miss StumbleUpon, I’m also saying I miss the internet as it used to be.

Back then (about when Mentos-and-Coke rocketed into the zeitgeist), the internet was a true world wide web of sites, owned and managed by people with diverse interests. People were weird and experimental online, mostly in a good way, and that made the internet endlessly interesting.

That’s something we still hold onto at Squarespace. We’re obsessive about the website and all the weirdness and interesting phenomena a website can convey. That’s our passion and we’re glad so many others feel the same way. And because we’re passionate about websites, we’re passionate about design.

That said, building and designing a website isn’t necessarily about being pixel-perfect. It can be, if that’s your passion, but good design is more akin to the adage that so many improv performers share with each other: “If you aren’t having fun, they aren’t having fun.”

If I can see your passion, your interest, or your personality on the page, that’s effective design.

One of my favorite zines is Cometbus, a zine about a Bay Area punk musician named Aaron Cometbus, who documented traveling across the United States on a Greyhound, seeing punk bands, and observing American life during the early ‘90s. The cover was often a black-and-white collage, his writing sometimes rough around the edges, and often he wrote about nothing in particular. But his passion came through every page. Despite an unpolished design aesthetic and penmanship, I and many others couldn’t wait to read and re-read Cometbus. Because Aaron was passionate about Cometbus, so were we.

Design, really, is about how much of yourself, in all your foible-ridden glory, you’re willing to put on the page. Yes, many of us have businesses and need to look professional online. We’re not all Bay Area punks traveling across Route 66 in the ‘80s and ‘90s, after all. But the quirks that surprise and delight our customers are what set us apart and make us accessible, whether that’s a button that opens a doorway into a new world, or a widget that streams BASE jumping.

Don’t delete the widget that sets you apart.

Stumble through Squarespace

Inspired by the button that started it all, we built a Squarespace version of Stumbling. Click through and discover real Squarespace websites you'd never find any other way.

Stumble
 

Frequently asked questions

What is StumbleUpon?

StumbleUpon was a web discovery tool that let users click a button to jump to random websites based on their interests. It launched in 2001 and became one of the most popular ways people found new content online before social media feeds took over.

What happened to StumbleUpon?

StumbleUpon shut down in 2018. Its founders relaunched a similar concept called Mix, which focused on curated content discovery rather than the original's random, button-click browsing experience.

What are some StumbleUpon alternatives?

A few tools carry on StumbleUpon's spirit of random discovery, including Mix, the direct successor built by StumbleUpon's original founders. If you’re looking for a new adventure, other random website buttons exist today like theuselessweb.com, boredbutton.com, and clicktheredbutton.com.

About the author

Tyler Huggins is Director of Global Content at Squarespace. He previously led growth at Acuity Scheduling. His work sits at the intersection of writing, design, and the future of content.

items.title: Why a Good-Looking Website Still Doesn’t Convert
items.body:
I love looking at beautifully designed apartments online. The kinds with intricate chairs no one sits in, one perfectly placed book on a coffee table, and a kitchen counter so pristine you start to wonder if the person who lives there has ever made toast. 

They’re beautiful, but every so often I look at one and think: where do I fit here?

Where are the shoes by the door? Where does the mail end up? A space can look completely finished and still leave you unsure what it would feel like to live there… and websites aren't so different.

We’ve gotten very good at recognizing what a good website is supposed to look like, and we’ve learned to judge them the way we judge a great apartment: by the immediate effect. The oversized photography, the perfect color palette, the sleek typography, the homepage with enough white space to make you think, oh, they have it together. But a good website, like a beautifully designed apartment, still has to work for the person stepping into it. If a visitor can admire your homepage but can’t figure out what you do, where to click, or why they should stay, then unfortunately, you’ve built a beautifully staged space, not a place they can picture themselves choosing.

That’s usually where the real decision starts. A visitor has already decided the site looks good, now they’re trying to figure out something more important: is this for me, do I understand what this business does, do I trust them, and what happens if I click?

A website can make a great first impression and still lose someone before they ever get to a yes. This is why.

Key takeaways

  • A stylish website can look complete while leaving a visitor’s question, like pricing, location, or what happens next, unanswered.
  • A page can have a call to action and still fail to convert if several competing links carry equal visual weight.
  • Generic trust signals, like a testimonial calling a business "great to work with," don't convince visitors the way a specific result does.
  • A low conversion rate isn't always a design problem, since mismatched traffic, like visitors from an unrelated referral or feature, can explain it too.
 

Design and conversion are two different jobs

A site can succeed at the first job and stall at the second, because each one needs something different from you.

Think about how quickly you decide you’re over a website or a business in general. A lot of the time, you can point to the exact reason: the price is higher than you expected, the business doesn’t ship to your area, or you need an appointment next week and the first opening is months away. Other times, it’s harder to pinpoint. You click around for a minute and somewhere along the way you just know it isn’t right for you.

You might keep reading and still not be sure if you’re actually their target customer. Maybe you open another tab to check reviews, or everything looks legitimate, but something is missing and you aren’t ready to hand over your credit card.

You make these tiny calculations all the time without calling them conversion decisions. Then you build your own website and forget that your visitors are doing the exact same thing.

That’s where a beautiful site can fool you a little. You already know your business, what the services include, why the product costs what it costs, and what someone should click next. You’ve probably stared at the homepage long enough to know exactly where everything lives.

The person landing there for the first time knows none of that.

They’re arriving with their own needs, doubts, budget, and distractions, maybe with three other tabs open. Looking polished gets you into consideration. It doesn’t make the decision for them.

Your homepage might be answering the wrong question

A photography website is an easy place to see this happen.

You land on a huge, beautiful wedding photo. The light is perfect and everyone looks polished and genuinely happy, just as you’d expect. You scroll and the next image is just as good. At this point, you know the photographer has taste. But say you’re planning a wedding in Brooklyn. Ten photographs later, you still don’t know if they shoot in New York. You can’t tell what you’re actually able to book, what the process looks like, or whether their starting price is close to your budget.

You came looking for a photographer and left only knowing they take excellent photographs.

Squarespace makes it easy to design a beautiful website quickly. That speed is part of the appeal, but it's easy to mistake “looks finished” for “is finished” before you’ve looked at the page the way a first-time visitor would. 

Demo copy can be short because it only has to demonstrate the layout. Demo photography is chosen because it fits that layout perfectly. Then you swap in your own images, write a few lines about your business, and everything still looks beautiful.

Visually, nothing looks wrong, so you might miss the practical details a visitor came looking for. Sometimes your headline just needs to be a little less mysterious. You might need to balance your photographs with more information about your style, where you operate, and what people are supposed to do if they want to hire you. Those are the insights that convince someone to click ‘Contact Me’ or ‘Book Now.’

If you need help finding the right words, Squarespace’s AI writer can help you draft that first pass.

Try Squarespace

There’s no visual hierarchy to highlight what’s important

Some websites make me feel like I’m being pulled in six different directions at once: book a call, read more, meet the team, join the newsletter, explore services, follow along.

All perfectly reasonable things to offer. All competing for attention at the same time. The visitor ends up deciding which part of your business matters most, not you. If someone is already reading about your consulting service and interested enough to move forward, they probably don’t need your newsletter, your Instagram, and your founder story all competing with the button that lets them hire you.

Visual hierarchy is what tells someone where to look first as they navigate your page. When everything is competing for that spot, nothing wins. Something has to win.

The same is true for effects. Video can be beautiful, animation can make a page feel alive, and a clever layout can make someone stop scrolling, but if they’re still scrolling to figure out what you do or where to click, that visual interest is working against you.

Decide what matters most on your page and make that one call to action visually obvious to guide your visitor to the next step.

Your trust signals are decorative, not specific

Personally, I want evidence before I spend money with someone I don’t know.

I look at reviews. I notice whether anyone has said something specific. If it’s a service, I want some idea of what happened for the people who hired them before. If it’s a product, I may be looking for the person who left three stars and wrote a dissertation-length review, because those are often more useful than the five-star ones.

A client testimonial that says someone was “amazing to work with” can feel great to receive and still leave a visitor with questions.

Amazing how, exactly?

Were they responsive when a project went sideways? Did they fix the problem? Did the project finish on time? Did someone hire them while feeling overwhelmed and walk away finally understanding what to do next? Specificity gives people something to believe.

The same is true of credentials, product descriptions, policies, case studies, and even basic information about how you work. The point isn’t to cover every inch of the site in social proof until it starts looking like you’re trying to win a court case. You just need to think about where a visitor might hesitate and whether you’ve given them anything useful on the other side of that hesitation.

Think about what would make you hesitate before buying from someone you don’t know, then look at your own site with that same question in mind.

Sometimes it’s not a design problem at all

If you changed your homepage for the fifth time and are seeing the same numbers afterward, your website design might not be the problem.

Traffic can be mismatched in ways no page update can fix. A wedding photographer who's only ever booked in Brooklyn might start showing up in a roundup post titled "Best Destination Wedding Photographers," shared by a blog that found their portfolio and made its own assumptions. The click comes from an audience that was never looking for a local photographer in the first place, so no amount of homepage work changes what brought them there.

The same goes for ecommerce. Someone can spend 20 minutes on your site comparing products, leave without buying anything, and still have gotten exactly what they came for. They may be researching, comparing prices, waiting until payday, or trying to remember if they already own something almost identical. I’ve talked myself out of purchases for less.

This is why conversion rate needs context. A low conversion rate isn’t automatically proof that something is wrong with your website design.

So before another round of font changes, look at where visitors are coming from and what brought them to the page before deciding your design has failed. Otherwise, you could spend another weekend rearranging a homepage that was doing its job perfectly well. If traffic is arriving through search, the page usually has a role to play; unclear copy is a fixable, on-page cause. If traffic is arriving through a referral, a feature, or an ad that targeted the wrong audience, the page isn’t responsible for who showed up.

Build a website someone can see themselves in

I still love those apartments.

I’ll probably keep saving photos of rooms where there appears to be nowhere to charge a phone, but I also know the difference between wanting to look at a room and wanting to live in it.

Your customers know the difference, too.

A good-looking website can make someone stop and look. What’s harder is giving them enough to picture themselves on the other side of whatever you’re offering. A customer can appreciate the photography, the type, the colors, all of it, and still never make the mental jump from “this is nice” to “this is for me.”

The right website builder can help design a site that looks like your brand and does its job at the same time. Squarespace’s Blueprint AI uses details about your business, goals, industry, and brand to recommend a personalized site structure, content, and visual direction. That alone can get you further than staring at a blank page and wondering where to begin.

At some point, a visitor’s admiration turns into consideration, and their question changes. It’s the one I had looking at those perfect apartments: where do I fit in?

Build a site that shows them.

Get Started
 

Frequently asked questions

Why isn't my website converting even though it looks good?

A website's design and its ability to convert visitors are two separate jobs. Design shapes how a visitor perceives a site in the first few seconds. Conversion depends on whether that visitor can find a clear answer to what they came looking for, such as pricing, location, or what happens after they take action. A site can succeed at the first job and still fall short on the second.

What's the most common reason a good-looking website doesn't convert?

Homepages often answer the wrong question. A visitor arrives asking something specific, like whether a business serves their area or what a service costs, and a polished homepage frequently answers a different question instead, like whether the business has good taste. This usually happens when a template's original demo content sticks around longer than it should.

How do I know if my call to action is clear?

A call to action is clear when it's the most visually obvious thing on the page, not one option competing equally with several others. If a page offers four or five links or buttons with the same visual weight, visitors might not choose any of them. Reducing competing options can help fix this.

What makes a testimonial or trust signal effective?

Specific outcomes convince visitors more than general praise. A testimonial that names a concrete result gives a visitor something to evaluate. A testimonial that only says a business was "great to work with" doesn't answer the follow-up questions a visitor is likely asking, like what problem got solved or whether the work finished on time.

Is a low conversion rate always a sign something's wrong with my website?

No. A low conversion rate can reflect mismatched traffic or normal browsing behavior rather than a design flaw. A business ranking for a broad or unrelated search term can attract visitors who were never a good fit, regardless of how the site looks. If a referral, a feature, or an unrelated audience sends visitors who were never a good fit, no amount of design work changes what brought them there. Checking where traffic comes from and what visitors searched for can clarify whether a redesign will help.

What are the most common small business website mistakes that hurt conversions?

The most common mistakes are homepages that don't answer a visitor's question, calls to action that compete with too many other links, and trust signals that stay vague instead of naming a specific result. Each one leaves a visitor without what they need to decide whether to stay.

About the author

Mika Kuyoro is the Partnerships Manager at Squarespace with a background in social media, community, and creative marketing. She develops content and marketing partnerships with creators, industry experts, and brands to help Squarespace reach and support entrepreneurs, creatives, and small business owners. Her work has also been featured in Marie Claire, and she has contributed guest writing on culture and community marketing to social marketing communities and publications on Substack.

seoData.seoDescription: Why isn't your website converting? A beautiful website can still have a low conversion rate. Here’s what could be going wrong.

items.title: What Makes a Good Website? A Must-Haves Checklist
items.body:
A good website helps visitors understand what you offer, makes it easy to take the next action, and provides a sense of trust and credibility for what you do. A flashy design and punchy content can set your website apart, but it also needs to be fast and secure, with clear navigation to boot. 

In other words, a good website isn't defined by any one feature. This can be a lot to consider if you’ve never made a website before, but whether you’re building your first website or your twentieth, the same core principles can ensure that your website is built to succeed. 

In a world where anyone can stand up a functional website in no time, these are the elements that will make yours stand out.

Key takeaways

  • A good website works as a system where navigation, speed, mobile design, and trust signals all work together.
  • Visitors should find your most important pages, like contact information and services, within one or two clicks.
  • Google measures site speed with Core Web Vitals: Largest Contentful Paint, Interaction to Next Paint, and Cumulative Layout Shift.
  • More than half of web traffic comes from mobile devices, so your site needs a responsive design that adapts automatically to any screen.
  • Clear next steps, useful content, and visible trust signals like reviews, credentials, and security badges, help turn visitors into customers.
 

1. Clear site navigation

Your site navigation is the menus, lists, and buttons that help a user (or a search engine) find their way through your website. To keep bounce rates low and visitors engaged, organize your content and pages for easy and intuitive browsing. Visitors should be able find what they're looking for within a couple of clicks at most.

Your most important pages should be the easiest to discover. The most visited pages on most websites are contact information and main services pages—these should be accessible from every other page in just one click. 

When it comes to site navigation, the best strategy is to keep things simple: descriptive labels are better than clever marketing copy when site visitors are trying to find an answer. 

For example, a hair salon looking to fill the calendar would be best served having information about their pricing and their stylists front and center, plus a clear way to book an appointment online. Having these links in the main menu of the website makes the user experience easier compared to burying a single “Book an Appointment” button at the bottom of a page.

2. Fast load times

A fast website should load in 2-3 seconds. If your website is slow to populate and leaves visitors waiting around, they might bounce instead, so it’s crucial to keep things running smoothly.

But how exactly do you know if your website is fast or slow? For Google search, this is typically broken down into three metrics known as “Core Web Vitals”:

  • Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) measures how long it takes for the largest visual element to fully render, whether it’s a hero image, video, or text block.

  • Interaction to Next Paint (INP) measures response times to clicks or taps on links, buttons, and other on-page elements. 

  • Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) measures visual stability once elements start loading on the user's screen. 

A reliable website builder like Squarespace handles a lot of page speed considerations for you, from hosting and servers to most of the core design layout. That said, there are still a few common culprits that slow site speeds that you can avoid to keep your website nimble: uncompressed images, in-line videos, excessive page length, and superfluous animations.

Try Squarespace

To reduce your page load times, start by keeping your pages short and to the point—fewer sections means less content to load. Limiting use of videos, GIFs, and other animated media can also keep things more efficient. 

Images should be compressed below 500 KB with a width of 1500px to 2500px whenever possible, while using .webp images for the quickest results. Third-party image editing and compression software can help with this, or use a free online image resizer. 

3. Mobile-friendly design

A mobile-friendly website means your content is easy to use, read, and navigate on a smartphone or tablet. More than half of all web traffic comes from mobile devices, so your website needs to work just as well on your customer’s phone as it does on your laptop. 

Most website builders include a responsive layout for your website, rather than a separate mobile version of all site pages. Responsive layouts adapt to screen size automatically without forcing the user to zoom in or turn their phone sideways for a better view. While you can edit the mobile layout of a page specifically in the editor, you don’t have to worry about maintaining two independent sites. 

Responsive sites handle much of the heavy lifting, including touchscreen navigation and button sizing, but these formatting tips can keep your website mobile friendly:

  • Keep your pages shorter for a better mobile experience (often under 5MB).

  • Avoid overly small or large font sizes. 

  • Double-check the ordering of copy, buttons, and other elements when the site switches to a mobile view. 

For example, your “Book an Appointment" CTA button might look great on desktop, but it won’t drive many clicks if it’s accidentally covered by an image or text on mobile.

4. Clear next steps and direction

Once a visitor lands on your website, the goal is to keep them there. Build your website to create engaged traffic that reads your content and acts on it. 

There’s more at play here than consumer psychology. A flashy animation or a brightly colored button can help attract eyeballs, but it’s not going to be enough to turn a landing into a lead for your business.

Similar to site navigation principles, it’s important to make it as easy as possible for a potential customer to take the action that you want. There should be no confusion about what you do, what you offer, and what you want the user to do with the information when they land on your site.

Say you sell bags of batch-roasted coffee. Make sure the price and the “add to cart” button are clearly visible and prominently displayed toward the top of your page. If you’re a therapist offering intro sessions, you want your calendar availability and booking button to be similarly noticeable.

This means not all links on your site should be displayed equally. If you need a hand crafting your next call to action (CTA), Squarespace compiled more than 30 CTA examples and best practices.

5. Useful content that answers visitors’ questions

A standard website should have a homepage, about us page, contact page, and products or services pages. Many websites may also include a blog, testimonials, or a portfolio. These pages all have unique content needs and serve distinct purposes on your site.

The key is to have your page content match the intent of the page as closely as possible. For example, your Contact Us page shouldn’t include an essay about your business philosophy or how you got started. Visitors want to find out how and when to contact you, or potentially send a message to you directly on the page.

At a minimum, useful site content is accurate, up to date, and at a reading level that’s easy to follow. If your coffee shop no longer offers that exclusive Colombian roast that’s prominently on your homepage, your customers will be disappointed when they arrive at the counter. An accountant’s blog post about 2026 tax code changes needs to be accessible to readers that don’t know the ins and outs of bookkeeping.

Consider this golden rule: identify what the reader wants to know when they land on this page, then target your content to that answer and cut as much fluff as possible. 

6. Effective and consistent design

At the simplest level, visual consistency should be the goal for your website and for your brand. The color palette, fonts, typography, and images should feel uniform and compatible across your pages.

A good website template does a lot of this for you, but several choices you make can matter as much as a good site layout and color scheme. For example, product photos, branded logos, and other images throughout the site should speak the same language. You want every element of your site to feel like a cohesive brand message.

Overall, you want to ensure that your site content is readable and well-spaced. A cluttered layout or an unexpected wall of text can undo the structure of a well-designed website.

7. Clear and transparent trust signals

A good website gives every user a legitimate reason to trust what they see. This starts with accurate contact details and digestible information about who you are and what you do.

Client testimonials, or product ratings and reviews if you're selling physical goods online, add social proof and increase confidence during the consideration phase. If you have industry credentials or credibility indicators, such as a state licensure or advanced degree, these are also important to display and verify.

Learn more about using client testimonials in your marketing strategy to build trust.

8. Optimized to be found everywhere

A good website should be discoverable everywhere, and that starts with search engine optimization (SEO). A reliable website builder handles your sitemap, robots.txt, technical SEO, and some elements of structured data for you automatically, but won’t be enough to cover your entire SEO strategy.

To make sure your website can be found in organic search and AI-generated results, start by including keyword phrases in your page titles, meta tags, and URLs. Tools like Google Search Console or other third-party platforms can assist with finding the right terms to inform your keyword optimization.

If you’re a brick-and-mortar business, a Google Business Profile that links to your website is also a must-have for map placements and local SEO.

Discover more tips to improve your on-page SEO and prepare your website for AI search.

9. Accessibility for every visitor

An accessible website is designed and coded in a way that remains functional for users of all abilities or disabilities. A good website builder covers most of the key fundamentals for you, but there are several choices that you can make to keep your website accessible.

Descriptive alt text for all images on your website helps vision-impaired visitors understand what’s pictured. Alt text is a short written description of an image that tools like screen readers use to describe what an image is about. Good alt text is accurate and clear, not stuffed with keywords for SEO.

Logical heading structure with clear H1, H2, and H3 tags also helps screen readers parse your content correctly, while helping search engine crawlers better understand your content, too.

Choose a color palette with enough contrast between text and background so visitors can read your content easily. This is especially important for text over images or colored backgrounds, where light gray text on a white background, or similar low-contrast combinations, can be hard to read. Check that product photos, logos, and other visual elements stay legible against your site’s background on both desktop and mobile screens.

Don’t treat accessibility like a compliance checkbox. An accessible website is a way to reach more customers and make sure that your business can serve everyone that walks through the door, virtual or otherwise. 

10. Visible security that builds trust

Every professional website needs a baseline of security to keep visitor data safe. While the technical details can be complex, these security standards are often handled automatically for you when you use a reliable website builder.

For starters, people look for the padlock icon in their browser’s address bar and a URL that starts with HTTPS. These trust signals are powered by an SSL certificate, which encrypts the connection between your site and your audience.

Maintaining these elements can help ensure visitors feel confident from the moment they land on your page. Without them, browsers may flag your site with safety alerts, which can quickly drive away potential visitors. 

Build a good website for your business

By following these fundamentals, anyone can build a beautiful website that helps their business succeed online. Treat these fundamentals as a formula instead of a checklist. All the parts work together to make your website genuinely good and worth visiting.

Frequently asked questions

What is a good website?

A good website makes it easy for visitors to understand who you are, what you offer, and what to do next. Clear navigation, focused copy, strong visuals, mobile-friendly design, and an obvious call to action all help visitors find what they need and take the next step.

How long should a website take to load?

Your website should load in 3 seconds or less to be considered fast. Keeping your pages short and targeted is a great first step to keeping load times down. Large images, videos, and animations can slow down a page, so optimize media and test your site on both desktop and mobile to catch performance issues before they cost you visitors.

How often should a website be updated?

Update your website whenever information changes, especially pricing, products, services, business hours, and contact details. Beyond those essential updates, review your site regularly to make sure the content still reflects your business and gives visitors accurate information. As a rule of thumb, a monthly audit of your website can help keep content fresh. 

Do I need a professional designer, or can I build a good website myself?

You can build a professional website yourself using a website builder, website templates, or AI tools. Consider hiring a web designer when you have a more complicated site or need more expertise in areas like user experience, branding, accessibility, or SEO.

How much should a website cost?

Website costs depend on how you build it and what features you need, including your website plan, domain, ecommerce tools, and any professional design services. Start with the features your website needs to accomplish its main goal, then add functionality as your business grows.
